source.title: Unlocking Basketball Athletic Performance: Countermovement Jump Rebound (CMJ-RE) Normative Reference Values Derived from Force Plate Data Across Seven NCAA Division-I Power Five Men’s College Basketball Teams

paper.citation: Berberet D., Petway A., Bell K., Gillen Z., Mundy P., Barrera H., et al. Unlocking Basketball Athletic Performance: Countermovement Jump Rebound (CMJ-RE) Normative Reference Values Derived from Force Plate Data Across Seven NCAA Division-I Power Five Men’s College Basketball Teams. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2025;5(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v5i1.555.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Can a countermovement-jump rebound test provide reliable reactive-strength information and position-specific reference values? Ninety-six NCAA Division I men’s basketball players from seven teams. Eighty-seven passed quality filters: 53 guards, 31 forwards, and three centers. Cross-sectional normative study using bilateral force plates. Examined 38 metrics, position differences, reliability, effort filters, and percentile bands.
paper.tldr: Position differences appeared in 37% of reported metrics; rebound jump height favored guards, while other significant metrics favored forwards. Mean ground-contact times exceeded 250 ms, so the test should not be treated as equivalent to a short-contact drop jump. Use the authors’ effort filters before interpreting CMJ-rebound data.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional normative study using bilateral force plates. Examined 38 metrics, position differences, reliability, effort filters, and percentile bands. Center comparisons were restricted by the very small subgroup.
paper.findings: Position differences appeared in 37% of reported metrics; rebound jump height favored guards, while other significant metrics favored forwards. Mean ground-contact times exceeded 250 ms, so the test should not be treated as equivalent to a short-contact drop jump. Eight metrics had coefficients of variation above 10%, making small changes difficult to interpret. Day-of-week effects appeared for modified RSI, while AM versus PM effects did not.
paper.limitations: Cross-sectional percentiles describe this sample and do not establish optimal values. Only one session was collected and familiarization remains a concern. Multiple comparisons and position imbalance increase false-positive risk. Basketball norms should not be used as football thresholds.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the authors’ effort filters before interpreting CMJ-rebound data. Prefer within-athlete trends and metric reliability over traffic-light norms, particularly when return-to-play decisions are involved.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, use the authors’ effort filters before interpreting CMJ-rebound data. Prefer within-athlete trends and metric reliability over traffic-light norms, particularly when return-to-play decisions are involved. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
